axis_categories.name: diegetic
axis_categories.description: The objective properties of the story's world — setting, physics, and stakes, independent of how the story about it is told.

axes.name: spatial setting
axes.description: The geographic and social type of place the story unfolds in.

axes.name: temporal setting
axes.description: Where the story sits on the timeline from historical to speculative.
examples: post-apocalyptic (after civilization's collapse, however far forward that falls)

scale.anchor_note: integer 0 = "deep past/prehistoric", integer 6 = "post-apocalyptic (after civilization's collapse, however far forward that falls)"; use the ordered examples above as anchors, half-steps allowed between adjacent anchors

axes.scale_caveat: 'alternate history' is a branch off the timeline, not a position on it -- score an alternate-history concept by the era it diverges from, and flag the counterfactual quality separately (tags/description) rather than forcing it onto this scale.

axes.name: ontology/physics
axes.description: How far the world's physical rules depart from consensus reality.
examples: mundane realism (no departure from consensus physics at all)
supernatural intrusion (one crack in an otherwise normal world)
high fantasy (fully alternate physics, but internally coherent)
surreal/dreamlike logic (physical law itself is unstable or inconsistent, not merely different)

scale.anchor_note: integer 0 = "mundane realism (no departure from consensus physics at all)", integer 5 = "surreal/dreamlike logic (physical law itself is unstable or inconsistent, not merely different)"; use the ordered examples above as anchors, half-steps allowed between adjacent anchors

axes.name: cosmology/meta-physics
axes.description: Whether the story implies a moral order behind events — a universe that rewards and punishes, or an indifferent one.

axes.name: scale of stakes
axes.description: The largest scope of consequence the plot threatens or promises, from a character's inner life up to civilization-wide.
examples: cosmic/existential (the fate of reality or existence itself)

scale.anchor_note: integer 0 = "internal/psychological (confined to one character's mind)", integer 6 = "cosmic/existential (the fate of reality or existence itself)"; use the ordered examples above as anchors, half-steps allowed between adjacent anchors

axes.name: milieu/social world
axes.description: The specific subculture or institutional world the story is embedded in, which supplies its texture, jargon, and norms.

axes.name: technological texture
axes.description: The prevailing level and character of technology available to characters in the world.
examples: post-scarcity (resource constraints no longer meaningfully shape life)

scale.anchor_note: integer 0 = "pre-industrial (no mechanized production at all)", integer 4 = "post-scarcity (resource constraints no longer meaningfully shape life)"; use the ordered examples above as anchors, half-steps allowed between adjacent anchors

axes.scale_caveat: 'anachronistic/mixed' (e.g. steampunk) blends eras rather than extending the scale -- treat as a categorical flag, not a position past post-scarcity.

axes.name: threat source
axes.description: Where the story's central danger originates in the world itself — the diegetic 'who or what.' Compare to the structural axis 'conflict type,' which frames that same threat in narrative terms (person vs. X).

axes.name: spatial confinement
axes.description: How much the world's geography constrains where the story can physically go.

scale.anchor_note: integer 0 = "open roaming (no meaningful geographic restriction)", integer 4 = "trapped/locked-room (a single, inescapable space)"; use the ordered examples above as anchors, half-steps allowed between adjacent anchors

axes.scale_caveat: 'branching map' (multiple paths/choices about where to go) describes topology, not raw openness, and overlaps with the interactivity axis 'branching structure' -- omitted here to avoid double-counting; use that axis for choice-of-route instead.

axis_categories.name: thematic
axis_categories.description: What the story is about, in the abstract — the ideas and values it dramatizes.

axes.name: core thematic axis
axes.description: The central binary tension the story dramatizes and ultimately takes (or refuses to take) a position on.
axes.encoding_note: This axis currently captures WHICH binary tension governs the story (a categorical pick). It does not capture WHERE on that tension the story lands (e.g. leaning toward 'chaos' vs 'order') -- that would be a second, ordinal judgment this schema doesn't yet model.

axes.name: ideological stance
axes.description: The political/social posture the story's resolution implies toward the existing order.

axes.name: views of institutions
axes.description: How the story portrays organized authority — governments, corporations, churches, police.

axes.name: views of violence
axes.description: The moral framing the story assigns to violent acts within it.

axes.name: view of history/fate
axes.description: The story's implicit theory of how time and events unfold.

axis_categories.name: structural
axis_categories.description: How the story is built — the mechanics of plot, cast, and time that shape it.

axes.name: plot architecture
axes.description: The overall template or shape the plot follows.

axes.name: conflict type
axes.description: The classic literary category of opposing force the protagonist struggles against. Compare to the diegetic axis 'threat source,' which names the specific in-world origin of that force.

axes.name: epistemic distribution
axes.description: Who knows what — the relative information held by the audience versus the characters.

scale.anchor_note: integer 0 = "audience > characters (dramatic irony)", integer 2 = "audience < characters (unreliable or withholding narrator)"; use the ordered examples above as anchors, half-steps allowed between adjacent anchors

axes.name: goal clarity
axes.description: How explicit and fixed the protagonist's objective is over the course of the story.
examples: single explicit goal (protagonist and audience both know exactly what's wanted)
no clear goal (drift/aimless, no defined want at all)

scale.anchor_note: integer 0 = "single explicit goal (protagonist and audience both know exactly what's wanted)", integer 4 = "no clear goal (drift/aimless, no defined want at all)"; use the ordered examples above as anchors, half-steps allowed between adjacent anchors

axes.name: causality
axes.description: How tightly plot events are bound together by cause and effect.

axes.name: closure
axes.description: The emotional and moral shape of the ending.

axes.name: temporal structure
axes.description: How the story orders and presents time to the audience, as distinct from the diegetic 'temporal setting' (when the story takes place).

axes.name: protagonist configuration
axes.description: The number and relational structure of the story's central character(s).

axes.name: agency
axes.description: How much control and competence the protagonist exercises over events.
examples: powerless/acted-upon (no meaningful influence over outcomes at all)

scale.anchor_note: integer 0 = "hyper-confident/exceptional (near-total control over outcomes)", integer 3 = "powerless/acted-upon (no meaningful influence over outcomes at all)"; use the ordered examples above as anchors, half-steps allowed between adjacent anchors

axes.scale_caveat: 'self-destructive/own worst enemy' is a distinct failure mode (capability turned against the self), not a lower point than powerless -- treat as a categorical flag if it applies, with lower confidence rather than a forced scale value.

axes.name: rules foregrounding
axes.description: How visible and explicit the story's internal rule system (magic system, game, law, procedure) is made to the audience.
examples: explicit ruleset the audience is meant to master (hard magic, game rules) -- the mechanics are the point
rules present but backgrounded (soft magic, atmosphere over mechanics)
no formal rule system (nothing resembling rules is ever exposed)

scale.anchor_note: integer 0 = "explicit ruleset the audience is meant to master (hard magic, game rules) -- the mechanics are the point", integer 2 = "no formal rule system (nothing resembling rules is ever exposed)"; use the ordered examples above as anchors, half-steps allowed between adjacent anchors

axis_categories.name: affective
axis_categories.description: How the story makes the audience feel, moment to moment and overall.

axes.name: primary affect
axes.description: The dominant emotional experience the story is designed to produce.

axes.name: affect trajectory
axes.description: How the intended emotion changes in intensity over the course of the story.

axes.name: tone/register
axes.description: The story's attitude toward its own material — sincere or knowing, light or heavy. Distinct from the formal axis 'language register,' which covers word choice and diction rather than attitude.
examples: deeply earnest/sincere (no ironic distance at all)
full camp/self-parody (maximal ironic distance from its own material)

scale.anchor_note: integer 0 = "deeply earnest/sincere (no ironic distance at all)", integer 4 = "full camp/self-parody (maximal ironic distance from its own material)"; use the ordered examples above as anchors, half-steps allowed between adjacent anchors

axes.scale_caveat: rewritten as single points along one sincerity spectrum (earnest -> camp); the original examples were binary pairs and couldn't anchor a scale. 'grim vs light' (heaviness) is a related but separate dimension this axis does not capture. Distinct from the formal axis 'reflexivity,' whose 'genre-aware parody' anchor is about formal self-awareness technique, not attitude.

axes.name: moral valence
axes.description: How clearly the story sorts characters and actions into good and bad.

axes.name: identification target
axes.description: Whose perspective the audience is invited to emotionally align with.

axes.name: somatic address
axes.description: What register of bodily or mental response the story primarily targets.

axes.name: distance
axes.description: How close the story invites the audience to feel to the events, versus preserving a sense of separation. Distinct from 'epistemic distribution,' which is about information rather than feeling.
examples: immersive/close (the audience is meant to feel inside the events)
alienated/estranged (the story deliberately holds the audience at arm's length)

scale.anchor_note: integer 0 = "immersive/close (the audience is meant to feel inside the events)", integer 2 = "alienated/estranged (the story deliberately holds the audience at arm's length)"; use the ordered examples above as anchors, half-steps allowed between adjacent anchors

axes.name: transgression level
axes.description: How much the story pushes against audience comfort or social norms.
examples: comfort-affirming (nothing here will unsettle a mainstream audience)
deliberately taboo-breaking (intentionally violates a core social or moral norm)

scale.anchor_note: integer 0 = "comfort-affirming (nothing here will unsettle a mainstream audience)", integer 3 = "deliberately taboo-breaking (intentionally violates a core social or moral norm)"; use the ordered examples above as anchors, half-steps allowed between adjacent anchors

axis_categories.name: formal
axis_categories.description: How the story is made and encountered — its craft choices and surface texture. For a text/IF engine, treat film-derived terms (camera, sound design) as their prose equivalents, noted below.

axes.name: medium/mode
axes.description: The delivery format the text takes. Kept broad in case the engine ever generates hybrid or non-prose forms.

axes.name: verisimilitude of style
axes.description: How closely the prose's rendering of reality mimics real-world texture versus stylizing or abstracting it.
examples: photorealistic/naturalistic detail (renders the world as lived experience would)
theatrical/heightened (emphasis and emotion pitched above naturalism, still representational)
abstract/impressionistic (mood and impression over literal detail)

scale.anchor_note: integer 0 = "photorealistic/naturalistic detail (renders the world as lived experience would)", integer 3 = "cartoonish/exaggerated (deliberately unrealistic distortion for effect)"; use the ordered examples above as anchors, half-steps allowed between adjacent anchors

axes.scale_caveat: 'abstract/impressionistic' and 'cartoonish/exaggerated' are different flavors of stylization (mood-abstraction vs. exaggeration-for-effect) rather than strictly sequential -- both are a bigger departure from naturalism than 'theatrical/heightened', but ordering between the two is a judgment call.

axes.name: iconography
axes.description: The recurring concrete objects and images that signal genre and setting at a glance.
examples: picket fences and porch lights (small-town Americana)

axes.name: sensory palette
axes.description: The dominant sensory quality of the prose's descriptive imagery -- its 'color' in the reader's mind's eye. Spans two related qualities, brightness and saturation; the examples below cover the corners of that space rather than a single line. (Renamed from 'visual palette' since a text medium engages more than sight.)

axes.name: scene staging/focalization
axes.description: The prose equivalent of camera grammar: how scenes are staged and framed. Spans two related qualities -- cutting rhythm (lingering vs. quick-cut) and framing distance (close/intimate vs. wide/panoramic); the examples below cover the corners of that space rather than a single line. (Renamed from 'camera/staging grammar.')
examples: long, lingering + close/intimate (extended dwelling inside one perspective)
quick-cut/montage + close/intimate (rapid shifts between subjective moments)
quick-cut/montage + wide/panoramic (rapid montage of establishing shots)

axes.name: soundscape idiom
axes.description: The auditory texture evoked through prose description — ambient sound, described music. Largely optional for a pure-text engine; more relevant if audio or voice output is ever added. (Renamed from 'sound design/score idiom.')

axes.name: language register
axes.description: The diction and formality of the prose itself — the vocabulary and sentence texture the reader encounters. Distinct from the affective axis 'tone/register,' which is about attitude rather than word choice.

axes.name: narration
axes.description: The point of view and mode of address used to tell the story.

axes.name: pacing/density
axes.description: The rhythm and information-density of the prose as experienced moment to moment.

scale.anchor_note: integer 0 = "contemplative/slow (lingers, minimal forward momentum)", integer 3 = "frenetic (constant, breathless forward momentum)"; use the ordered examples above as anchors, half-steps allowed between adjacent anchors

axes.scale_caveat: 'rhythmic/lyrical' describes prose quality (verse-like cadence), not speed, and can occur at any point on this scale -- treat as a categorical flag if it applies, not a position past frenetic.

axes.name: length/unit
axes.description: The intended overall size and release format of the piece.

scale.anchor_note: integer 0 = "short story/vignette (a single sitting)", integer 5 = "open-ended/persistent (no defined endpoint at all)"; use the ordered examples above as anchors, half-steps allowed between adjacent anchors

axes.scale_caveat: the serial modes represent scope-over-time rather than single-work size, so they're placed by convention rather than strict length measurement. 'open-ended/persistent' is a different kind of extreme than the others: length becomes unbounded, not merely large.

axes.name: violence explicitness
axes.description: How graphically violence is depicted on the page.

scale.anchor_note: integer 0 = "none", integer 3 = "graphic/detailed (rendered in full physical detail)"; use the ordered examples above as anchors, half-steps allowed between adjacent anchors

axes.name: sexual explicitness
axes.description: How graphically sexual content is depicted on the page.

scale.anchor_note: integer 0 = "none", integer 3 = "graphic/detailed (rendered in full explicit detail)"; use the ordered examples above as anchors, half-steps allowed between adjacent anchors

axes.name: reflexivity
axes.description: How aware the text is of its own status as a constructed story.
examples: transparent (no acknowledgment) -- never signals it's a constructed story
genre-aware parody (knowingly mimics and exaggerates the conventions it's told in)
full meta-fiction (breaks the fourth wall) -- characters or narration directly address the audience or the text's own construction

scale.anchor_note: integer 0 = "transparent (no acknowledgment) -- never signals it's a constructed story", integer 3 = "full meta-fiction (breaks the fourth wall) -- characters or narration directly address the audience or the text's own construction"; use the ordered examples above as anchors, half-steps allowed between adjacent anchors

axes.scale_caveat: distinct from the affective axis 'tone/register,' whose 'camp/self-parody' anchor is about attitude, not this axis's formal acknowledgment-of-construction.

axis_categories.name: extra-textual
axis_categories.description: How the story situates itself relative to the real world — its audience, tradition, and context of production.

axes.name: target audience
axes.description: The intended readership by age and sophistication.
examples: children (no content requiring adult context or discretion)

scale.anchor_note: integer 0 = "children (no content requiring adult context or discretion)", integer 3 = "adult (no content restriction intended)"; use the ordered examples above as anchors, half-steps allowed between adjacent anchors

axes.scale_caveat: 'scholarly/niche' describes intended sophistication, not age-appropriateness, and isn't a further point past 'adult' -- treat as a categorical flag if it applies (e.g. an adult work aimed at a specialist audience).

axes.name: function/use context
axes.description: The primary purpose the piece is meant to serve beyond the story itself.

axes.name: production tier
axes.description: The implied scale of resources and craft behind the piece — mainly a flavor and tone signal for a text generator rather than a literal budget.
examples: no-budget/amateur (little to no resources or craft polish)

scale.anchor_note: integer 0 = "no-budget/amateur (little to no resources or craft polish)", integer 3 = "prestige/lavish (maximal resources and craft investment)"; use the ordered examples above as anchors, half-steps allowed between adjacent anchors

axes.name: distribution/venue
axes.description: Where and how the piece is imagined to reach its audience.

axes.name: corpus lineage/intertext
axes.description: The piece's relationship to a prior tradition or specific influential works it is responding to.

axes.name: national/regional tradition
axes.description: The storytelling tradition and convention set the piece draws its structure and sensibility from.

axes.name: star/auteur persona
axes.description: Whether the piece is built as a vehicle for a signature voice or persona. For a generative engine, express this as an archetype rather than naming a real person.
examples: vehicle for a charismatic archetype (e.g. wisecracking action lead)
house style of a genre-auteur archetype (e.g. moody neo-noir stylist)

axes.name: cultural moment
axes.description: The real-world cultural or historical backdrop the piece is implicitly conversing with.

axes.name: relation to reality
axes.description: How the piece frames its own truth-claim relative to real events.

axes.name: franchise position
axes.description: Where the piece sits relative to other installments in a series.

axis_categories.name: interactivity
axis_categories.description: PROPOSED NEW CATEGORY — how the audience acts on and within the story. This is the one dimension a pure prose taxonomy can't cover, and it's arguably central for an engine named stratum-if. Delete this block if interactivity is out of scope for this generator.

axes.name: branching structure
axes.description: The shape of the choice graph the player moves through.

axes.name: choice granularity
axes.description: How frequently, and at what scale, the player is asked to make decisions.

axes.name: player-protagonist relationship
axes.description: How the player relates to the character(s) they control.
examples: defined character with their own voice

axes.name: failure & consequence model
axes.description: How the story handles player mistakes or 'bad' choices.
examples: no fail state (every choice remains valid; nothing is punished)
permadeath, no retry (failure is total and irreversible)

scale.anchor_note: integer 0 = "no fail state (every choice remains valid; nothing is punished)", integer 3 = "permadeath, no retry (failure is total and irreversible)"; use the ordered examples above as anchors, half-steps allowed between adjacent anchors

axes.scale_caveat: 'consequences accumulate silently (delayed payoff)' describes timing (when consequences land), not severity, and can pair with any point on this scale -- treat as a categorical flag if it applies, not a position past permadeath.

axes.name: ending multiplicity
axes.description: How many distinct endings the branching structure produces and how they relate to each other.
examples: single ending, choices affect texture only
many endings on a spectrum (best to worst)
open-ended/no true ending (closure itself is never defined)

scale.anchor_note: integer 0 = "single ending, choices affect texture only", integer 4 = "open-ended/no true ending (closure itself is never defined)"; use the ordered examples above as anchors, half-steps allowed between adjacent anchors

axes.scale_caveat: 'open-ended/no true ending' is a different kind of extreme than 'combinatorial' -- not simply more endings, but the absence of a defined endpoint at all.

encoding_legend.ordinal: Single meaningful scale. Judge model outputs an integer (or half-step) index against the axis's own ordered `examples` list per `scale.min`/`scale.max`. Normalize to [0,1] via value/scale.max for storage and distance math.
encoding_legend.nominal: No defensible single order. Judge model generates a short descriptive text targeted at this axis, which is then embedded and (ideally) reduced via per-axis PCA before use in distance math.
encoding_legend.scale_caveat: Present on some ordinal axes. Flags a named quality that doesn't sit cleanly on the scale itself (a different, orthogonal quality) -- the judge model should set 'applies: false' for concepts matching the flagged quality specifically, rather than forcing them onto the scale.
